thread.title: MARKET SNAPSHOT: Stocks Edge Higher As Defensive Sectors Take Lead

author: morningstar.com
title: MARKET SNAPSHOT: Stocks Edge Higher As Defensive Sectors Take Lead
text:
By Sue Chang, MarketWatch , Chris Matthews
Apple shares fall after Trump suggests possibility of tariffs on iPhones
Stocks bounced back from early losses to trade higher Tuesday as gains in so-called defensive sectors helped to offset fresh anxieties that a near-term resolution to trade tensions between the U.S. and China can be reached.
How are benchmarks performing?
The S&P 500 index gained 5 points, or 0.2%, to 2,678 with consumer staples and utilities, which are favored during times of economic uncertainty, leading the winners.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 47 points, or 0.2%, to 24,685 and the Nasdaq Composite Index added 8 points, or 0.1%, to 7,090.
What's driving the market?
President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal, in an interview (https://www.wsj.com/articles/trump-expects-to-move-ahead-with-boost-on-china-tariffs-1543266545?mod=searchresults&page=1&pos=1) published late Monday, that it is "highly unlikely" that he would accept Beijing's request to hold off on increasing tariff rates on Chinese goods from the beginning of January 2019, raising some doubts about prospects for a detente between the world's two largest economic superpowers when Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet in Buenos Aires later this week. The pair are set to discuss trade on the sidelines of a meeting of the Group of 20 nations.
Trump said that if talks with his Chinese counterpart don't go well that he could put tariffs on the rest of Chinese imports that are currently not subject to duties. "If we don't make a deal, then I'm going to put the $267 billion additional on" at a tariff rate of either 10% or 25%, he told WSJ.
Animosities over trade between the U.S. and China have been among the central concerns for investors recently because an intensification of hostilities could precipitate a slowdown in China and the rest of the world.
Investors are also digesting comments from Federal Reserve No. 2 Richard Clarida, who continued to present a relatively dovish stance (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/fed-policy-should-be-aimed-at-sustaining-expansion-clarida-2018-11-27) in a Monday morning speech to a conference sponsored by The Clearing House in New York, ahead of a Fed policy meeting later this month, when the central bank is widely expected to raise interest rates.
Market participants, however, are eager for more clarity as to the Fed's plan for interest rate increases in 2019, and on this point, Clarida said incoming data "supports the case for gradual policy normalization" next year, while emphasizing that the federal-funds rate much closer to the "neutral level," at which the Fed will stop raising rates, than it was when it began hiking in 2015. "How close is a matter of judgment, and there is a range of views on the FOMC," he said.
Read:Stock-market investors cheer Italy, Brexit headlines for a change--but it might not (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/investors-cheerful-about-italy-brexit-for-a-change-2018-11-26)
What are strategists saying?
"Psychology is the main force driving markets lower," Matt Lloyd, chief investment strategist at Advisors Asset Management, told MarketWatch. "We're a bunch of long-tailed cats in a room full of rocking chairs" waiting for the worst to happen, he said.
While an escalating trade war could hurt some corporate profits, Lloyd said, other factors, like low unemployment, rising wages, and a resilient global economy -- as evidenced by 80% of purchasing manager surveys around the world indicating improving economic conditions -- should overwhelm trade headwinds, Lloyd argued.
"As for Apple, and the impact from possible tariffs...any negative effects are likely to be overstated given that the firm was able to absorb the impact of lifting the ceiling price on its most expensive iPhone model by much more than that with its recent upgrades," wrote Michael Hewson, chief market strategist at CMC Markets UK, in a note.
Which stocks are in focus?
Apple Inc. shares (AAPL) dropped 0.5% after Trump said during The Wall Street Journal interview that tariffs could also be placed on iPhones (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-stock-falls-after-hours-as-trump-mentions-potential-tariffs-on-iphones-2018-11-26)and laptop computers imported from China if the U.S. decides to put tariffs on additional goods.
Microsoft Corp.(MSFT) shares are in focus as the software giant aims to claim the title of the world's largest company. The software-and-services firm closed Monday with a market capitalization just $11 billion, or 1.3% shy of Apple's market cap, currently the world's largest firm by market value. Microsoft shares were up 0.6%.
United Technologies Corp. (UTX) fell 5.4% after it announced plans to break its company in to three parts.
Shares of General Motors Co. (GM) fell 2.7% a day after it closed at a three-month high following the announcement of cost-cutting measures (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/gm-stock-rises-4-on-restructuring-plan-calling-for-layoffs-cost-cutting-2018-11-26) that included layoffs and plant closures. Trump on Monday ripped GM's plans (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/trump-today-president-threatens-to-close-border-with-mexico-as-he-demands-congress-fund-wall-2018-11-26), telling the Journal he told Barra she should stop making cars in China and replace lost production in Ohio. National Economic Council chairman Larry Kudlow also said Trump is looking at withdrawing subsidies (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/kudlow-hints-us-may-withdraw-electric-car-subsidies-after-gm-job-cut-announcement-2018-11-27) on electric cars in the wake of GM's announcement.
Tiffany & Co. (TIF) slid 1% ahead of the jewelry merchant's third-quarter earnings report to be released before the market open Wednesday. The stock has been under pressure in recent weeks as a supply glut (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-11-12/de-beers-is-said-to-make-big-cuts-in-low-quality-diamond-prices) for low-end diamonds has forced prices to fall.
Shares of Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. (BMY) declined 3.7%, after the company reported the failure of a study of a prospective skin-cancer drug Monday evening.
What data are in the spotlight?
Home prices across the country are rising at the slowest pace in nearly two years (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/house-price-growth-slows-to-nearly-two-year-low-as-case-shiller-makes-the-slowdown-official-2018-11-27), according to the S&P/Case-Chiller 20-city Index, released Wednesday morning.
How are other markets trading?
Asian markets started strong (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/asian-markets-cool-off-as-investors-await-trump-xi-meeting-2018-11-26) but cooled on fears over rising U.S.-China trade tensions. Japan's Nikkei rose 0.6%, but Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index finished down 0.2%, while China's Shanghai Composite Index also ended slightly lower.
European markets declined (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/european-stocks-weighed-by-trade-worries-regional-politics-2018-11-27) with the Stoxx Europe 600 falling 0.6%.
Crude oil reversed direction to trade lower (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/oil-attempts-to-hold-ground-on-hopes-for-production-cut-2018-11-27) after it notched its best single-day gains in 8 weeks. Gold was on track for a third straight losing session (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/gold-silver-manage-slim-gains-ahead-of-fed-speakers-trade-developments-2018-11-27) while the U.S. dollar saw a modest rise (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/sterling-under-pressure-amid-new-attacks-on-mays-brexit-deal-2018-11-27).
--Mark DeCambre contributed to this report
(END) 15:00 ET (20:00
